danish.title: Tolvte bog (1812) — Kapitel 4
paragraphs: Det er naturligt for os, der ikke levede i de dage, at forestille os, at da halvdelen af Rusland var erobret og indbyggerne flygtede til fjerne provinser, og den ene udskrivning efter den anden blev foretaget til forsvaret af fædrelandet, da var alle russere fra den største til den mindste udelukkende optaget af at ofre sig, redde fædrelandet eller græde over dets fald. Fortællingerne og beskrivelserne fra den tid taler uden undtagelse kun om selvopofrelse, patriotisk hengivenhed, fortvivlelse, sorg og russernes heltemod. Men sådan var det i virkeligheden ikke. Det ser sådan ud for os, fordi vi kun ser den almene historiske interesse fra den tid og ikke alle de personlige menneskelige interesser, folk havde. Men i virkeligheden overskyggede disse personlige øjeblikkets interesser altid de almene i en grad, der forhindrede den offentlige interesse i overhovedet at blive mærket eller bemærket. De fleste mennesker på den tid skænkede ingen opmærksomhed til begivenhedernes almene gang, men lod sig kun styre af deres private interesser, og det var netop disse mennesker, hvis virke på den tid var mest nyttigt.

De, der forsøgte at forstå begivenhedernes almene gang og deltage i dem med selvopofrelse og heltemod, var samfundets mest unyttige medlemmer; de så alting på hovedet, og alt, hvad de foretog sig for det fælles bedste, viste sig at være nyttesløst og tåbeligt — som Pierres og Mamónovs regimenter, der plyndrede russiske landsbyer, og det charpi, de unge damer lavede, som aldrig nåede de sårede, og så videre. Selv de, der var glade for intellektuel snak og for at udtrykke deres følelser, og som drøftede Ruslands stilling, indførte uvilkårligt i deres samtale enten et skær af forstillelse og falskhed eller unyttig fordømmelse og vrede rettet mod folk, der blev beskyldt for handlinger, ingen overhovedet kunne være skyldige i. I historiske begivenheder gælder forbuddet mod at spise af Kundskabens Træs frugt i særlig grad. Kun ubevidst handling bærer frugt, og den, der spiller en rolle i en historisk begivenhed, forstår aldrig dens betydning. Forsøger han at indse den, er hans anstrengelser frugtesløse.

Jo tættere en mand var knyttet til de begivenheder, der fandt sted i Rusland, desto mindre indså han deres betydning. I Petersborg og i provinserne fjernt fra Moskva græd damer og herrer i militsuniformer for Rusland og dets ældgamle hovedstad og talte om selvopofrelse og lignende; men i hæren, der trak sig tilbage bag Moskva, talte og tænkte man kun lidt på Moskva, og da de fik øje på de nedbrændte ruiner, svor ingen at hævne sig på franskmændene, men tænkte på deres næste sold, deres næste kvarter, på marketenderersken Matrjósjka og den slags.

Da krigen havde ramt Nikolaj Rostov, mens han var i tjenesten, deltog han tæt og længe i forsvaret af sit fædreland, men gjorde det tilfældigt, uden noget mål om selvopofrelse, og han så derfor på, hvad der skete i Rusland, uden fortvivlelse og uden tungsindigt at martres af det. Havde man spurgt ham, hvad han tænkte om Ruslands tilstand, ville han have sagt, at det ikke var hans sag at tænke over det, at Kutuzov og andre var der for det, men at han havde hørt, at regimenterne skulle gøres fuldtallige, at kampene nok ville fortsætte længe endnu, og at som tingene stod, ville han sandsynligvis have kommandoen over et regiment om et par år.

Da han betragtede sagen på den måde, erfarede han, at han blev sendt til Vorónezj for at købe remonter til sin division, ikke blot uden beklagelse over at blive forhindret i at deltage i det forestående slag, men med den største glæde — som han ikke skjulte, og som hans kammerater fuldt ud forstod.
Få dage før Borodinó-slaget modtog Nikolaj de nødvendige penge og bevillinger, sendte nogle husarer forud og tog selv af sted med postheste til Vorónezj.

Kun den, der har oplevet det — det vil sige har tilbragt nogle måneder uafbrudt i felttog og krig — kan forstå den fryd, Nikolaj følte, da han slap fri af det område, der var dækket af hærens fouragering, forsyningstog og lazaretter. Da han — fri for soldater, vogne og de beskidte spor af en lejr — så landsbyer med bønder og bondekoner, herregårde, marker med græssende kvæg og poststationer med sovende stationsmestre, frydede han sig, som om han så alt dette for første gang. Hvad der i lang tid særligt forundrede og glædede ham, var kvinderne, unge og sunde, uden et dusin officerer, der gjorde kur til hver eneste af dem; kvinder, der oven i købet var glade og smigrede over, at en forbireisende officer spøgte med dem.

I det bedste humør ankom Nikolaj om aftenen til et hotel i Vorónezj, bestilte ting, han længe havde savnet i felten, og gik næste dag, helt nyligt barberet og i gallauniform, som han ikke havde båret længe, hen for at melde sig hos myndighederne.

Militschefen var en civil general, en gammel mand, der tydeligvis var tilfreds med sin militære titel og rang. Han modtog Nikolaj brysk (idet han forestillede sig, at dette var karakteristisk militært) og udspurgte ham med vigtig mine, som overvejede han begivenhedernes almene gang med fuld ret til at godkende og misbillige. Nikolaj var i så godt humør, at dette blot morede ham.

Fra militschefen kørte han til guvernøren. Guvernøren var en livlig lille mand, meget jævn og elskværdig. Han anviste stutterier, hvor Nikolaj kunne skaffe heste, anbefalede ham en hestehandler i byen og en godsejer sytten kilometer uden for byen, der havde de bedste heste, og lovede at hjælpe ham på enhver måde.
»De er grev Ilja Rostovs søn? Min kone var nær veninde med Deres moder. Vi har åbent hus om torsdagen — i dag er det torsdag, så kom endelig, helt uformelt,« sagde guvernøren ved afskeden.

Straks efter at have forladt guvernøren lejede Nikolaj postheste og kørte med sin skvadrons kvartermester i galop ud til godsejeren sytten kilometer borte, der havde stutteriet. Alt syntes ham behageligt og let i den første del af opholdet i Vorónezj, og som det sædvanligvis sker, når man er i godt humør, gik alt godt og let.

Godsejeren, som Nikolaj besøgte, var ungkarl, en gammel kavalerist, hesteven, sportsmand, ejer af noget hundredårigt brændevin og noget gammelt ungarsk vin, med et hyggeligt rum, hvor han røg, og ejer af nogle pragtfulde heste.

Med ganske få ord købte Nikolaj sytten udvalgte hingste for seks tusind rubler — til, som han sagde, at tjene som prøver på hans remonter. Efter at have spist og nydt lidt for rigeligt af den ungarske vin — og med venskabeligt kindkys med godsejeren, som han allerede stod på den fortroligste fod med — galopperede Nikolaj ad forfærdelige veje tilbage i det bedste humør, idet han ustandseligt drev på kusken for at nå til guvernørens selskab.
Da han havde skiftet tøj, hældt vand over hovedet og parfumeret sig, ankom Nikolaj til guvernørens temmelig sent, men med talemåden »bedre sent end aldrig« på læberne.

Det var ikke et bal, og der var heller ikke meldt dans, men alle vidste, at Katerína Petróvna ville spille valse og skotsk dans på klavichorden, og at der ville blive danset, og så var alle kommet som til et bal.

Provinslivet i 1812 gik stort set sin vante gang, men med den forskel, at der var livligere i byerne på grund af tilstrømningen af mange velhavende familier fra Moskva, og som i alt, hvad der foregik i Rusland på den tid, var der en særlig letsindighed, en »hvad rager det os«-stemning, og den uundgåelige snak, der ellers drejede sig om vejret og fælles bekendte, handlede nu om Moskva, hæren og Napoleon.
Det selskab, der var samlet hos guvernøren, var det bedste i Vorónezj.

Der var mange damer og nogle af Nikolajs bekendtskaber fra Moskva, men ingen mænd, der på nogen måde kunne måle sig med denne kavaler af Sankt Georgsordenen, denne husarremonteofficer, den godmodige og velklædte grev Rostov. Blandt mændene var en italiensk krigsfange, en officer fra den franske hær; og Nikolaj følte, at denne fanges tilstedeværelse øgede hans egen betydning som russisk helt. Italieneren var så at sige en krigstrofæ. Nikolaj mærkede det, det syntes ham, at alle betragtede italieneren i samme lys, og han behandlede ham venligt, men med værdighed og tilbageholdenhed.

Så snart Nikolaj trådte ind i sin husaruniform og udbredte en duft af parfume og vin omkring sig og havde udtalt ordene »bedre sent end aldrig« og hørt dem gentaget flere gange af andre, flokkedes folk om ham; alle øjne var rettet mod ham, og han følte straks, at han var trådt ind i sin rette plads i provinsen — som en alles yndling: en meget behagelig stilling, og berusende efter hans lange afsavn. Ved poststationerne, på kroerne og i godsejerens hyggelige rum havde stuepigerne følt sig smigrede af hans opmærksomhed, og her hos guvernøren var der ligeledes (som det forekom Nikolaj) et uudtømmeligt antal smukke unge kvinder, gifte og ugifte, der utålmodigt ventede på hans opmærksomhed. Kvinderne og pigerne flirtede med ham, og fra den første dag var folk optaget af at få denne flotte unge husarforvovent gift og bosat. Blandt disse var guvernørens kone selv, der bød Rostov velkommen som en nær slægtning og kaldte ham »Nikolaj«.

Katerína Petróvna spillede virkelig valse og skotsk dans, og dansen begyndte, og Nikolaj betog provinsselskabet yderligere med sin behændighed. Hans særligt frie måde at danse på overraskede dem endog alle. Nikolaj var selv temmelig overrasket over den måde, han dansede på den aften. Han havde aldrig danset sådan i Moskva og ville endda have anset en så fri og ugenert stil for upassende og uraffineret, men her følte han, at det var hans pligt at forbløffe dem alle med noget usædvanligt, noget de ville opfatte som det normale i hovedstaden, skønt det var nyt for dem i provinsen.

Hele aftenen viste Nikolaj opmærksomhed mod en blåøjet, buttet og tiltalende lille blondine, kone til en af provinsembedsmændene. Med unge mænds naive overbevisning, når de er i godt humør, om at andre mænds hustruer er skabt for dem, forlod Rostov ikke damen og behandlede hendes mand på en venlig og sammensvoren måde, som om de begge uden at tale om det vidste, hvor udmærket Nikolaj og damen ville passe sammen. Manden syntes dog ikke at dele denne overbevisning og forsøgte at opføre sig mut over for Rostov. Men sidstnævntes godhjertethed var så grænseløs, at selv manden til tider ufrivilligt lod sig smitte af Nikolajs gode humør. Hen mod aftenens slutning, efterhånden som konens ansigt blev mere og mere rødmende og livligt, blev mandens mere og mere trist og alvorligt, som om der var en given mængde livlighed imellem dem, og når konens andel voksede, mindskedes mandens.

english.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: We who didn't live through those days naturally picture them this way: half of Russia conquered, the inhabitants fleeing to distant provinces, one levy after another raised to defend the fatherland, and every Russian, great or small, busy only with sacrificing himself, saving his country or weeping over its fall. The tales and descriptions of that time, without exception, speak only of Russian self-sacrifice, patriotic devotion, despair, grief and heroism. But it was not really so. It looks that way to us because we see only the general historic interest of the time and miss the personal, human interests people actually had. Yet the personal interests of the moment are so much stronger than the general ones that they always stop the public interest from being felt or even noticed. Most people then paid no attention to the general course of events and followed only their private interests, and these were the very people whose activity in that period was the most useful.

The people who tried to understand the general course of events and join in it with self-sacrifice and heroism were the most useless members of society. They saw everything upside down, and everything they did for the common good turned out useless and foolish — like Pierre's and Mamonov's regiments, which looted Russian villages, or the lint the young ladies prepared that never reached the wounded, and so on. Even people who loved intellectual talk and expressing their feelings, and who discussed Russia's position at the time, could not help bringing into their talk either a touch of pretense and falsehood or pointless condemnation and anger aimed at people accused of things no one could possibly be guilty of. In historic events the ban on eating the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge applies with special force. Only unconscious action bears fruit, and whoever plays a part in a historic event never understands what it means. If he tries to understand it, his efforts come to nothing.

The more closely a man was involved in the events then taking place in Russia, the less he understood their significance. In Petersburg and in the provinces far from Moscow, ladies and gentlemen in militia uniforms wept for Russia and its ancient capital and talked of self-sacrifice and so on. But in the army that had retreated beyond Moscow there was little talk or thought of Moscow, and when the soldiers caught sight of its burned ruins, no one swore to take revenge on the French. They thought about their next pay, their next quarters, Matreshka the vivandière, and things of that sort.

The war had caught Nicholas Rostov in the service, so he took a close and lasting part in the defense of his country. But he did it casually, with no thought of self-sacrifice, and so he watched what was happening in Russia without despair and without gloomily racking his brains. Had anyone asked what he thought of the state of Russia, he would have answered that it was not his business to think about it; Kutuzov and others were there for that. He had heard, however, that the regiments were to be filled up to full strength, that the fighting would probably go on a long time yet, and that, such being the case, he might very well command a regiment in a couple of years.

Since he saw the matter this way, he felt no regret when he learned that he was being sent to Voronezh to buy remounts for his division, and so would miss the coming battle. He felt the greatest pleasure. He did not hide it, and his comrades understood it perfectly.
A few days before the battle of Borodino, Nicholas received the money and warrants he needed, sent some hussars ahead, and set out for Voronezh with post horses.

Only someone who has been through it, who has spent some months without a break in the atmosphere of campaigning and war, can understand how delighted Nicholas was to get out of the area stripped by the army's foraging parties and crowded with its supply trains and hospitals. Free of soldiers, wagons and the filthy traces of a camp, he saw villages with peasants and peasant women, country houses, fields with cattle grazing, posthouses with the stationmasters asleep, and he rejoiced as if seeing it all for the first time. What surprised and delighted him most, for a long while, were the women. They were young and healthy, with no dozen officers courting each one, and they were pleased and flattered when a passing officer joked with them.

In the highest spirits, Nicholas reached a hotel in Voronezh at night and ordered things he had long done without in camp. The next day, very clean-shaven and in a full-dress uniform he had not worn for a long time, he went to present himself to the authorities.

The militia commander was a civilian general, an old man who was clearly pleased with his military title and rank. He greeted Nicholas curtly (thinking that was how soldiers behaved) and questioned him with an air of importance, as though he were weighing the general state of affairs and had every right to approve and disapprove. Nicholas was in such high spirits that it only amused him.

From the commander of the militia he drove to the governor. The governor was a brisk little man, very simple and friendly. He named the stud farms where Nicholas could get horses, recommended a horse dealer in the town and a landowner fourteen miles out who had the best horses, and promised to help him in every way.

"You are Count Ilya Rostov's son? My wife was a great friend of your mother's. We are at home on Thursdays, and today is Thursday, so please come and see us quite informally," said the governor as he said goodbye.

Nicholas left the governor's, hired post horses at once, took his squadron quartermaster along and drove at a gallop to the landowner with the stud, fourteen miles off. In that first part of his stay in Voronezh everything seemed pleasant and easy to him, and, as usually happens when a man is in a pleasant mood, everything went well and easily.

The landowner Nicholas went to see was a bachelor, an old cavalryman, a horse lover and sportsman. He had some century-old brandy and old Hungarian wine, a snuggery where he smoked, and some splendid horses.

Nicholas bought seventeen picked stallions for six thousand rubles, with very little talk — to serve, as he put it, as samples of his remounts. After dinner, having taken rather too much of the Hungarian wine, he exchanged kisses with the landowner, with whom he was already on the friendliest terms, and galloped back over abominable roads in the brightest of moods. He kept urging the driver on so as to reach the governor's party in time.
He changed, poured water over his head and scented himself, and arrived at the governor's rather late, but with the phrase "better late than never" on his lips.

It was not a ball, and no dancing had been announced, but everyone knew that Catherine Petrovna would play waltzes and the écossaise on the clavichord and that there would be dancing, so everyone had come as if to a ball.

Provincial life in 1812 went on much as usual, except that it was livelier in the towns because many wealthy families had come from Moscow. A special recklessness showed in everything done in Russia then, an "in for a penny, in for a pound — who cares?" spirit. And the inevitable small talk now turned not on the weather and mutual acquaintances but on Moscow, the army and Napoleon.
The company gathered at the governor's was the best in Voronezh.

There were a great many ladies and a few of Nicholas' Moscow acquaintances, but no man there could in any way rival the cavalier of St. George, the hussar remount officer, the good-natured and well-bred Count Rostov. Among the men was an Italian prisoner, an officer in the French army, and Nicholas felt that the prisoner's presence added to his own importance as a Russian hero. The Italian was, as it were, a war trophy. Nicholas felt this, and it seemed to him that everyone saw the Italian the same way, so he treated him cordially, though with dignity and restraint.

As soon as Nicholas entered in his hussar uniform, spreading around him a fragrance of perfume and wine, said "better late than never" and heard others repeat it several times, people clustered around him. All eyes turned on him, and he felt at once that he had stepped into his proper position in the province, that of universal favorite. It was a very pleasant position, and intoxicatingly so after his long privations. At posting stations, at inns and in the landowner's snuggery, maidservants had been flattered by his notice, and here too at the governor's party there were (as it seemed to Nicholas) an inexhaustible number of pretty young women, married and unmarried, impatiently waiting for him to notice them. The women and girls flirted with him, and from the first day the people concerned set about getting this fine young daredevil of a hussar married and settled down. Among them was the governor's wife herself, who welcomed Rostov as a near relative and called him "Nicholas."

Catherine Petrovna did play waltzes and the écossaise, and the dancing began, and Nicholas won over provincial society still more with his agility. His unusually free way of dancing astonished them all. Nicholas was rather astonished at it himself that evening. He had never danced like that in Moscow, and he would have thought such a free and easy manner improper and in bad taste. But here he felt it was his duty to amaze them all with something out of the ordinary, something they would have to accept as the regular thing in the capital even though it was new to them in the provinces.

All evening Nicholas paid attention to a blue-eyed, plump and pleasing little blonde, the wife of one of the provincial officials. With the naive conviction of young men in a merry mood that other men's wives were created for them, Rostov did not leave the lady's side and treated her husband in a friendly, conspiratorial way, as if, without saying it, they both knew how splendidly Nicholas and the lady would get on together. The husband, however, did not seem to share that conviction and tried to behave morosely toward Rostov. But Nicholas' good-natured naivety was so boundless that sometimes even the husband gave way, in spite of himself, to Nicholas' good humor. Toward the end of the evening, though, as the wife's face grew more flushed and animated, the husband's grew more and more melancholy and solemn, as if there were only a fixed amount of animation between them, and as the wife's share grew, the husband's shrank.
